To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) living in deprived neighbourhoods is not associated with worse access to resources from social networks, (2) there is no evidence that people in deprived neighbourhood are better connected to social networks than people in other neighbourhoods, and (3) living in deprived areas is associated with worse access only to a few services, but not to the majority of them.
(i) living in a deprived neighbourhood does not provide greater access to resources from social networks, and (ii) living in a more deprived neighbourhood does not mean worse access to services.
living in deprived neighbourhoods does not provide greater access to services or social networks, and that it does not lead to a greater level of social support.
In summary, our research is concerned with

two key issues: first, the extent to which living in a deprived neighbourhood affects access to resources from social networks; second, the extent towhich living in a deprived area affects access to resources through service providers.
the extent to which social mix policies are justified by the need to improve the lives of poor people.
the extent to which neighbourhoods matter for the well-being of individuals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
neighbourhoods have little effect on social networks and on access to services.
social mix policies do not have any significant effects on access to resources in social networks or services.
there are no neighbourhood effects on access to resources from either social networks or services.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social mix debate has not been well served by the evidence base.
neighbourhood social mix is neither a good nor a bad thing.
neighbourhoods do matter, but the evidence is not consistent with claims about the benefits or harms of neighbourhood social mix.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the neighbourhood effect is a very weak one, at least for the UK.
social mix is not a simple good or bad thing.
the neighbourhood effects on resources are complex and that they are mediated by the characteristics of the individuals and the resources in question.
